To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

raised temperature at the time of filleting has an impact on the development of rigor mortiss, which subsequently affects muscle pH, reflective properties, and visual perception during 14 days storage.

raised muscle temperature at point of commercial filleting of Atlantic salmon significantly affects development of rigor morti, and subsequently affects the reflective properties of fillet surface and development of muscle pH during storage.
increased muscle temperature at point of processing has no effect on fillet quality for raw Atlantic salmon fillets but has an effect on cold-smoked fillet quality.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a new aspect of the filleting process that has been overlooked until now.
the impact of increased muscle temperatures at the point of fish filleting on filleting quality of raw- or cold smoked Atlantic salmon.
the effect of raised muscle temperature at the filleting point on subsequent quality changes in raw- and cold smoked fillets during refrigeration.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
increased muscle temperature during filleting affects visual perception, muscle pH, and reflective properties of cold-smoked filleted raw-Atlantic salmon.

the effect of raised temperature at the point filleting on filleting and subsequent storage quality is dependent on the type of product, the type and duration of processing, and the storage conditions.
raised muscle temperature at the time of filleting affects the development of pH, which subsequently affects the visual perception and sensory attributes of raw- and especially cold-smoked salmon.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
increased muscle temperature at point of processing is an important quality factor to consider when processing prerigor filleted Atlantic salmon.

raised muscle temperature at the time of filleting has a significant impact on fillet quality, but the effect is more pronounced for visual perception of cold-smoked filleted salmon than for raw fillets.
increased muscle temperature at point of processing is of no importance for raw- and cold smoked fillet quality, except for the visual perception.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the temperature of the fish at the point of slaughter should be as low as possible to avoid a subsequent rise in temperature during the filleting process.
the muscle temperature at the time of filleting has to be carefully considered to ensure that the fillets meet the quality demands from the market.
the temperature of filleted fish should not exceed 9 ℃ during the initial 3 h post mortem.
